about: Machine-readable list of the example labs. Paths are relative to this file.

labs.name: A 1 Mbit bottleneck
labs.about: A fast school LAN reaches a server through one slow cable (1 Mbit/s, with a small queue, like a cheap uplink). A short burst fits; a long one overflows the queue and frames are dropped. Look at the drops field in the result.

labs.name: Count to infinity (teaching scenario, engine only)
labs.about: A triangle of routers with triggered updates off: after a LAN cut, the false route circulates and its metric climbs from 3 to 16.

labs.name: DHCP through a relay
labs.about: The only DHCP server sits in the server room. Student PCs are on another network, behind router R1. DHCP broadcasts cannot cross a router, so R1 relays them to the server, which picks an address from the pool for the PC's network.

labs.name: DHCP, then a router to the server network
labs.about: PC1 has no address. A DHCP server on the same LAN hands it one (and names the router as the default gateway). After that, PC1 can reach a web server network on the far side of router R1. DHCP broadcasts do not cross a router, so each LAN needs its own DHCP server (or a relay).

labs.name: Router on a stick
labs.about: R routes between VLANs 10 and 20 over one trunk cable using 802.1Q subinterfaces eth0.10 and eth0.20; its untagged eth0 is on the native VLAN 1. SW1 and SW2 are VLAN-aware switches joined by a trunk. E is in VLAN 30, which R has no subinterface for.

labs.name: Layer 3 switch
labs.about: SW1 is a Layer 3 switch: SVIs vlan10, vlan20 and vlan30 route between its VLANs, and a static route sends 10.9.0.0/24 to router R on VLAN 30. SW2 is a plain VLAN switch on a trunk.

labs.name: LACP: three cables as one port-channel
labs.about: Hosts A and C on SW1, B and D on SW2. SW1:p3-p5 and SW2:p3-p5 are bundled into port-channel Po1 (802.3ad). Each frame leaves over one member cable, chosen by the MAC-address hash; cut a cable and the others carry on.

labs.name: Switch triangle, no spanning tree
labs.about: Three switches cabled in a ring, with no spanning tree. One broadcast (the ARP request inside a ping) goes round and round. Watch the frame counts.

labs.name: Switch triangle, with spanning tree
labs.about: The same ring of three switches, but spanning tree is on. SW1 has the lowest bridge ID and becomes the root; one port on SW3 blocks, so the ring is cut into a line. Pings wait for the ports to finish listening and learning (about 8 seconds with these shortened timers).

labs.name: MAC aging
labs.about: Two switches with different aging times. After a pause one switch has forgotten where a host is and floods the next frame to everyone, while the other still forwards it to one port.

labs.name: Port security
labs.about: A small switch with two hosts plugs into a port that allows one MAC address. The first host heard is secured; the second is dropped and counted.

labs.name: RIP on a chain of three routers (poisoned reverse)
labs.about: Three routers learn each other's networks with RIPv2. Cut a cable: the route is poisoned (metric 16), then garbage collected, and returns when the cable is restored.

labs.name: Two LANs and a router: ping, traceroute, DNS
labs.about: Students on 10.0.0.0/24, servers on 10.1.0.0/24, one router between them. Ping crosses the router, traceroute shows it as the first hop, and DNS turns a name into an address.

labs.name: Rapid spanning tree: fast failover
labs.about: A triangle of rapid-spanning-tree switches: cut the root port's cable and the blocked (alternate) port takes over at once, with no forward-delay wait. Edge ports (portfast) forward immediately.

labs.name: STP topology change
labs.about: Cut a cable in a spanning-tree triangle: TCN BPDUs and the topology-change flag make every switch age out MAC entries after one forward delay instead of the normal aging time.

labs.name: TCP across a router
labs.about: A client, a router and two echo servers (TCP port 7). SERVER has a default route back to the client; BROKEN has no gateway, so it never answers and the client's SYN is retransmitted.

labs.name: Two VLANs across a trunk
labs.about: Two switches joined by one trunk cable that carries VLAN 10 (Sales) and VLAN 20 (Labs). Hosts in the same VLAN can talk even on different switches; hosts in different VLANs cannot, even though they share an IP subnet and a cable. (Crossing between VLANs needs a router: see the intervlan-roas and l3-switch labs.)

labs.name: Access lists on a router
labs.about: A router filters between a host and a server with in and out access lists: allowed DNS, UDP and echo pass, everything else hits the implicit deny and the sender gets 'administratively prohibited'. TCP connects are refused at once, like on Linux.

labs.name: NAT on a router
labs.about: Private hosts behind a router share its public address (overload), one host has a fixed public address, and the outside reaches an inside web server through a forwarded port. Connection tracking brings the replies home.
